_doc: Sổ mẫu câu theo chức năng (xưởng nội dung, scripts/factory/comm.mjs – docs/CONTENT-FACTORY.md §4). Sinh tự động, đừng sửa tay; sửa → content/factory/review.jsonl.

functions.name: Asking the price of something

formal: Excuse me, could you tell me the price of this?
How much is this item, please?
Could you tell me how much this costs?
neutral: How much is this, please?
How much are these apples?
What is the price of this bag?

example.en: Excuse me, how much is this, please?
It is fifteen dollars.
Okay, I will take it.
Great. Cash or card?

avoid.right: How much is this?
avoid.why: Use 'much' for money and price, not 'many'.

functions.note: Use 'is this' for one thing and 'are these' for multiple items.

functions.name: Asking someone to repeat or speak more slowly

formal: Could you please repeat that?
Pardon me, could you speak more slowly?
Could you say that once more, please?
neutral: Can you repeat that, please?
Sorry, can you speak more slowly?
Could you say that again, please?

responses: Of course. I said your train is at five.
Yes, sorry! I will speak slower.

example.en: Sorry, can you speak more slowly?
Of course. The bus arrives at ten o'clock.
Can you repeat that, please?
Sure, it arrives at ten o'clock.

avoid.right: Sorry, could you say that again?
avoid.why: 'What?' alone sounds abrupt and impolite to English speakers.

functions.note: Saying 'Sorry?' with rising intonation is a quick, natural way to ask someone to repeat what they just said.

functions.name: Asking where a place is

formal: Excuse me, could you tell me where the station is?
Pardon me, do you know where the restroom is?
Could you please direct me to the museum?
neutral: Excuse me, where is the bus stop?
Is there a bank near here?
Where can I find a pharmacy?

responses: It is next to the supermarket.
It is five minutes from here.

example.en: Excuse me, where is the bus stop?
It is across the street, near the shop.
Is it far from here?
No, just two minutes away.

avoid.right: Where is the bus stop?
avoid.why: Singular countable places require an article like 'the' or 'a'.

functions.note: Start with 'Excuse me' before asking a stranger for directions.

functions.name: Greeting someone

formal: Good morning.
Good afternoon.
It is nice to see you.
neutral: Hello.
Hello, how are you?
Good to see you.

responses: Hello! Good to see you too.

example.en: Good morning. How are you today?
Good morning! I am very well, thank you.
It is nice to see you.
Nice to see you too.

avoid.right: Good evening, how are you?
avoid.why: Use 'good night' only when leaving or going to sleep.

functions.note: Use 'Good morning' before 12:00 and 'Good afternoon' after 12:00. 'Hi' is the most common casual greeting.

functions.name: Introducing a friend to someone

formal: May I introduce my colleague, Anna?
I would like you to meet Anna.
This is Anna, our new team member.
neutral: This is my friend, Anna.
Anna, meet Sam. Sam, this is Anna.
Have you met my friend Anna?

responses: Hello Anna, nice to meet you.
Hi Anna! Good to meet you.

example.en: This is my friend, Anna.
Hi Anna! Nice to meet you.
Anna, meet Sam. Sam, this is Anna.
Great to finally meet you.

avoid.right: This is my friend Anna.
avoid.why: Use 'this is' rather than 'here is' when introducing people.

functions.note: Use 'This is [Name]' when introducing someone standing next to you. It works in both social and work settings.

functions.name: Introducing yourself

formal: Hello, my name is Alex Reed.
Allow me to introduce myself, I am Alex.
Nice to meet you, I am Alex Reed.
neutral: Hello, I am Alex.
My name is Alex. Nice to meet you.
I am Alex. Pleased to meet you.

example.en: Hello, I am Alex.
Nice to meet you, Alex. I am Sam.
Nice to meet you, too.
Welcome to our class.

avoid.wrong: I introduce myself, I am Alex.
avoid.right: Hello, my name is Alex.
avoid.why: We rarely say 'I introduce myself' in natural spoken English.

functions.note: Saying 'Nice to meet you' is standard after hearing someone's name for the first time.

functions.name: Ordering food and drink

formal: May I please have the chicken salad?
I would like a glass of water, please.
Could I have a coffee, please?
neutral: Can I have a tea, please?
I would like the soup, please.
A cheese sandwich for me, please.

example.en: Hello, are you ready to order?
Can I have a tea, please?
With milk and sugar?
Just milk, please.

avoid.right: Can I have a coffee, please?
avoid.why: 'I want' sounds too direct and rude to servers.

functions.note: Always add 'please' at the end of an order to sound polite.

functions.name: Saying goodbye

formal: Goodbye. Have a nice day.
It was nice meeting you.
Have a pleasant evening.
neutral: Goodbye.
See you tomorrow.
Take care.

example.en: Goodbye. Have a nice day.
Thank you! You too.
See you tomorrow.
Yes, see you!

avoid.right: See you tomorrow.
avoid.why: You can only see someone again in the future.

functions.note: 'Bye' is friendly and safe in almost every everyday situation. 'Goodbye' sounds slightly more final or polite.

functions.name: Saying you do not understand

formal: Pardon me, could you repeat that?
I am sorry, I do not understand.
Could you speak more slowly, please?
neutral: I do not understand.
Sorry, what does that mean?
Can you say that again, please?

responses: Yes, I will say it again.

example.en: Take bus number twelve to the station.
I am sorry, I do not understand.
Take bus twelve. It goes to the trains.
Ah, okay. Thank you!

avoid.right: I do not understand.
avoid.why: Use 'do not' with the base verb 'understand', not 'am not'.

functions.note: Saying 'Sorry?' with rising intonation is very common and polite in everyday English.

functions.name: Saying sorry for a small mistake

formal: Please excuse me.
I beg your pardon.
Pardon me, please.
neutral: I am sorry.
Sorry about that.
I am so sorry.

example.en: Oops, sorry! I took your pen.
That is okay. I have another one.
Here it is. Thank you.
No problem at all.

avoid.wrong: I am sorry for drop your book.
avoid.right: I am sorry for dropping your book.
avoid.why: Use an -ing verb after the preposition 'for'.

functions.note: Use 'sorry' for everyday accidents. Keep your voice light so the other person knows it is not a serious problem.

functions.name: Saying thank you and replying

formal: Thank you very much for your help.
I am very grateful, thank you.
Thank you kindly.
neutral: Thank you very much.
Thank you for that.
Thanks a lot.

example.en: Here is your ticket and your change.
Thank you very much.
You are welcome. Have a nice trip.
Thank you, you too.

avoid.right: Thank you.
avoid.why: Say either 'thanks' or 'thank you', never combine them with an 's'.

functions.note: The standard reply to 'thank you' is 'you are welcome'.

functions.name: Accepting an invitation

formal: Thank you, I would be delighted to attend.
It would be a pleasure to join you.
Thank you, I accept with pleasure.
neutral: I would love to, thanks.
That sounds great, thank you.
Yes, I will definitely be there.

responses: Great, I will send you the details.
Excellent, I look forward to it.

example.en: We are having lunch together. Would you like to come?
That sounds great, thank you.
Great, we are meeting at twelve.
Sounds good, see you there.

avoid.right: Yes, I would love to.
avoid.why: 'I like' talks about general hobbies; use 'I would love to' to accept an offer.

functions.note: After saying yes, show enthusiasm by adding a positive comment like 'That sounds great' or 'Thanks for inviting me'.

functions.name: Apologising

formal: Please accept my sincere apologies for the delay.
I apologise for any inconvenience caused.
I am extremely sorry for being late to the meeting.
neutral: I am really sorry about that.
Sorry for keeping you waiting.
I am sorry, that was my fault.

responses: That is quite all right, do not worry.
It happens, do not worry about it.

example.en: I am really sorry about that.
No problem at all.
I dropped the glass by accident.
Do not worry, I will clean it up.

avoid.right: I apologise.
avoid.why: 'Apologise' is a verb, so do not use 'am' before it.

functions.note: Use 'I am sorry' for everyday mistakes, and save 'I apologise' for more serious situations.

functions.name: Asking for directions

formal: Excuse me, could you tell me how to get to the station?
Could you please direct me to the museum?
Pardon me, would you know where the post office is?
neutral: Excuse me, where is the nearest bank?
How do I get to the bus stop from here?
Is there a supermarket near here?
informal: Do you know where the park is?
Are we near the train station?

responses: Go straight on and turn left at the lights.
It is just around the corner on your right.
Sorry, I do not know this area.

example.en: Excuse me, where is the nearest bank?
Go straight on and turn left at the lights.
Is it far to walk?
No, it is only two minutes away.

avoid.right: Where is the hotel?
avoid.why: Singular countable nouns like hotel need an article such as the or a.

functions.note: Start with 'Excuse me' before asking a stranger for directions to sound polite.

functions.name: Asking for permission

formal: May I leave the room for a moment?
Would it be possible for me to use this phone?
Might I ask a question?
neutral: Could I borrow your pen, please?
Can I open the window?
Is it okay if I sit here?

responses: I am sorry, but someone is sitting there.

example.en: Excuse me, is it okay if I sit here?
Yes, of course. Nobody is here.
Thank you very much.
You are welcome.

avoid.right: May I sit here?
avoid.why: Never use 'to' after modal verbs like 'may', 'can', or 'could'.

functions.note: Use 'May I' with teachers, managers, or strangers in formal situations.

functions.name: Booking an appointment by phone

formal: I would like to arrange an appointment, please.
Could you tell me your earliest availability?
I am calling to schedule a consultation.
neutral: I would like to book an appointment for Tuesday.
Do you have any openings this afternoon?
Can I make an appointment with the doctor, please?
informal: Can I come in tomorrow morning?
Do you have anything free today?
Can I book a slot for this Friday?

responses: Certainly, what time suits you best?
We have an opening at two o'clock.
Could I take your name, please?

example.en: Can I make an appointment with the doctor, please?
Certainly, what time suits you best?
Do you have anything available tomorrow morning?
Yes, we have an opening at ten o'clock.

avoid.right: I would like to make an appointment.
avoid.why: 'I want' sounds abrupt and demanding when requesting a service.

functions.note: Always confirm the date and time before hanging up to prevent misunderstandings.

functions.name: Checking in at a hotel

formal: Good afternoon, I have a reservation under the name of Smith.
Could we please check in? The booking is for two nights.
We have a room reserved under John Davis, please.
neutral: Hello, I would like to check in, please.
Hi, I have a booking under Anna Miller.
We are checking in, the name is Taylor.
informal: Hi there, checking in for Sam Brown.
Hi, we have got a room booked here.
Just checking in, name is Lee.

responses: Welcome. May I see your passport, please?
Here is your key card. Breakfast is on the first floor.
Your room is not quite ready yet.

example.en: Hello, I would like to check in, please.
Welcome. May I see your passport, please?
Sure, here it is.
Thank you. Here is your key card for room 204.

avoid.wrong: I want my key, I booked.
avoid.right: Hello, I have a booking, please.
avoid.why: Demanding a key sounds rude; state that you have a booking instead.

functions.note: Give your surname clearly when checking in so staff can find your booking quickly.

functions.name: Declining an invitation politely

formal: Thank you, but I am unable to attend.
I appreciate the invitation, but I have another commitment.
I am sorry, but I cannot make it that day.
neutral: I am sorry, but I cannot come.
I would love to, but I am busy then.
Thanks for asking, but I cannot make it.
informal: Wish I could, but I cannot.

responses: That is okay, thanks for telling me.

example.en: Are you coming to my dinner party on Friday?
I would love to, but I am busy then.
That is okay, thanks for telling me.
Have a wonderful time anyway!

avoid.wrong: I cannot come because I don't want.
avoid.right: I cannot come, but thank you.
avoid.why: Stating that you do not want to go sounds very rude.

functions.note: Always thank the person before or after saying no so you remain polite.

functions.name: Disagreeing in a simple way

formal: I’m afraid I disagree.
With respect, I see it differently.
I’m not convinced.
neutral: I don’t think that’s right.
I see it another way.
That’s not how I understand it.

example.en: I’m not convinced that the test will be easy.
Why do you think that?
Because the material is quite tough.
I see, maybe we can study together.

avoid.wrong: I disagree with you very much.
avoid.right: I strongly disagree.
avoid.why: "Very much" sounds unnatural; use stronger adverbs.

functions.note: Disagree politely, especially in formal contexts.

functions.name: Giving directions

formal: Go straight ahead until you reach the crossroads.
Take the second turn on your right-hand side.
Continue past the station and it will be on your left.
neutral: Go straight on and turn left at the lights.
Take the first street on the right.
Walk down this road for two minutes.
informal: Just head down here and turn left.
It is right around the corner.
Keep going until you see the big park.

example.en: Excuse me, where is the nearest bank?
Go straight on and turn left at the lights.
Is it far from here?
No, it takes only two minutes to walk there.

avoid.right: Turn left.
avoid.why: Use the simple adverb 'left' or 'on your left' for direction commands.

functions.note: Use clear landmarks like traffic lights, corners, or stations to make directions easier to follow.

functions.name: Inviting someone out

formal: Would you care to join us this evening?
I would like to invite you to dinner.
Would you be interested in attending?
neutral: Would you like to come with us?
Do you want to see a film tonight?
Are you interested in joining us?
informal: Come to the cinema with me!

responses: I would love to, thank you.
I am sorry, but I am busy.

example.en: Would you like to come with us to the park?
I would love to, thank you.
Great, we are leaving in ten minutes.
Perfect, I will get my coat.

avoid.wrong: Do you want go to the cinema?
avoid.right: Do you want to go to the cinema?
avoid.why: Remember to include 'to' before the main verb after 'want'.

functions.note: Use 'Would you like to...' as a polite and safe standard invite for both friends and colleagues.

functions.name: Making a plan to meet

formal: Would tomorrow suit you?
Could we schedule a time to meet?
What time would be convenient for you?
neutral: Are you free this afternoon?
Can we meet at two o'clock?
What time works best for you?
informal: Do you want to hang out later?

responses: I cannot make it then, sorry.

example.en: Are you free this afternoon?
Yes, I am free after three o'clock.
Can we meet at four at the cafe?
Yes, that time is fine. See you then.

avoid.right: Can we meet tomorrow at five?
avoid.why: Use 'can' or 'shall' to make a question for future plans.

functions.note: Always confirm the exact time and place at the end of the conversation so both people agree.

functions.name: Making a polite request

formal: Could you please assist me with this?
Would you mind helping me, please?
May I trouble you for some assistance?
neutral: Could you help me, please?
Can you please pass that to me?
Could you tell me the time, please?
informal: Can you give me a hand?
Help me with this, will you?

responses: I am sorry, but I cannot right now.

example.en: Excuse me, could you help me, please?
Sure, what do you need?
I cannot find the tea bags.
They are right here on shelf two.

avoid.right: Could you give me that book, please?
avoid.why: Using an imperative alone sounds like an order instead of a request.

functions.note: Use 'could' instead of 'can' when you want to sound more polite.

functions.name: Making a suggestion

formal: May I suggest that we schedule a meeting?
Perhaps we could consider a different route?
I would like to propose a new idea.
neutral: How about we try the new cafe?
What if we start early?
Maybe we should ask for help.
informal: Why don’t we watch a film?

example.en: May I suggest that we take the train instead of the bus?
Sounds good.
Great, I’ll book the tickets.
Thanks, that helps a lot.

avoid.right: I suggest we go.
avoid.why: 'Suggest' is followed by a clause, not 'to' + infinitive.

functions.note: After 'suggest' use 'that' clause or a gerund.

functions.name: Offering help

formal: May I assist you with that?
Would you like any assistance today?
Please let me know if I can help you.
neutral: Can I help you with anything?
Do you need any help?
Would you like a hand with that?

responses: Yes, please. That is very kind.
No, thank you. I am fine.

example.en: Those boxes look heavy. Would you like a hand with that?
Yes, please. That is very kind.
Where should I carry them?
Just put them on the table, thanks.

avoid.wrong: I must help you with your bag.
avoid.right: Can I help you with your bag?
avoid.why: Do not force help on people; ask questions to give them a choice.

functions.note: Saying 'Need a hand?' is common and friendly among coworkers and friends.

functions.name: Reporting a simple problem

formal: I am afraid there seems to be a problem with the air conditioning.
Excuse me, I believe there is an error on our bill.
Pardon me, the television in my room does not appear to be working.
neutral: Excuse me, the shower is not working.
There is a problem with my order, this is cold.
This shirt is damaged, look at this mark.
informal: The light will not turn on.

responses: I am so sorry, I will fix that right away.
Let me speak to the manager about that.
I will bring you a fresh one immediately.

example.en: Excuse me, the shower is not working.
I am so sorry, I will fix that right away.
Thank you, there is no hot water.
I will send someone to your room now.

avoid.right: The machine is not working.
avoid.why: Use the negative verb 'is not working' to describe a broken item.

functions.note: Start with 'I am afraid' or 'Excuse me' to report problems politely without sounding angry.

functions.name: Asking for another size or returning an item

formal: Could I please exchange this item for a larger size?
I would like to return this shirt, please.
Could you tell me if you have this in medium?
neutral: Do you have this in a size ten?
Can I try this on in a smaller size?
I want to return this, please.
informal: Got this in a bigger size?
Can I swap this for a small?
Can I bring this back if it does not fit?

responses: Let me check the stockroom for you.
Yes, do you have your receipt?
I am sorry, we have sold out of that size.

example.en: Do you have this in a size ten?
Let me check the stockroom for you.
Thank you, I will wait here.
Here you go, we had one left.

avoid.right: I want to exchange this shirt.
avoid.why: Use 'exchange' with 'to', or say 'swap' in casual speech.

functions.note: Shops usually ask for a receipt when you want to return or swap an item.

functions.name: Asking for advice

formal: Could you advise me on how to improve my CV?
I would appreciate your guidance regarding the project.
Might you have any recommendations for a good dentist?
neutral: What would you suggest?
Do you have any advice?
Any tips for staying focused?
informal: What do you think I should do?

responses: You could try updating the layout.
I think you should practice more regularly.

example.en: Could you advise me on which language course to choose?
You could try the evening class; it fits most schedules.
Thanks, that sounds perfect.
Happy to help!

avoid.wrong: I need advice from you to do this.
avoid.right: I need your advice on this.
avoid.why: 'Advice' is a noun; use 'your advice' rather than 'advice from you'.

functions.note: 'Advise' is a verb; 'advice' is the noun you receive.

functions.name: Asking for clarification

formal: Could you clarify what you meant by that statement?
Would you mind elaborating on the last point?
May I ask you to explain this part further?
neutral: Can you explain that again?
What do you mean by this?
Could you give an example?

responses: Sure, I meant that we need more data.
Of course, let me give you an example.
I’ll explain it in a different way.

example.en: Can you explain that again?
Sure, I meant that we need more data.
Could you give an example?
I’ll explain it in a different way.

avoid.right: Explain that to me.
avoid.why: English uses a preposition after 'explain'.

functions.note: Use 'explain that to me' or 'clarify what you meant' for clear requests.

functions.name: Asking for a favour

formal: Would you be able to assist me with this report, please?
May I kindly ask you to review my presentation?
Could I request your help in organising the meeting?
neutral: Can you help me move these boxes?
Would you mind covering my shift tomorrow?
Could you give me a hand with this task?
informal: Hey, can you do me a favour?
Could you grab me a coffee?

responses: Sorry, I'm a bit busy right now.
I can do it after lunch.

example.en: Could you give me a hand with this task?
Of course, what do you need?
I need to copy these files onto the server.
I'll do it right away.

avoid.right: Can you help me?
avoid.why: Modal verbs are followed directly by the base verb.

functions.note: Match the level of politeness to your relationship with the person.

functions.name: Changing an arrangement

formal: I would like to propose an amendment to our schedule.
Due to unforeseen circumstances, we need to reschedule our meeting.
May I suggest moving the appointment to a later date?
neutral: Can we change the time?
I need to shift our plans.
Is it possible to meet tomorrow instead?
informal: How about we do it later?

responses: I’m sorry, I’m not available then.
Let me check and get back to you.

example.en: We were supposed to meet today at 3 p.m.
Is it possible to meet tomorrow instead?
Yes, tomorrow at the same time works for me.
Great, see you then.

avoid.right: Is it possible to meet tomorrow instead?
avoid.why: Frames the change as a request, not a demand.

functions.note: When altering plans, phrase it as a polite request.

functions.name: Changing the subject

formal: If I may, let's turn our attention to…
Perhaps we could discuss… instead
May I suggest we move on to…
neutral: Let's talk about…
How about we change the topic to…
What do you think about…
informal: Speaking of that, did you hear…

example.en: If I may, let's turn our attention to the budget.
Sure, that's fine.
The budget figures are ready for review.
Got it.

avoid.right: I would like to change the subject.
avoid.why: Missing article and polite phrasing.

functions.note: Use a transition phrase to signal a shift politely.

functions.name: Congratulating someone

formal: Congratulations on your achievement.
Please accept my sincere congratulations.
I would like to commend you on your success.
neutral: Well done!
Congrats!
Nice job!

example.en: Well done on finishing the project!
Thanks, it was a team effort.
Your hard work really paid off.
I’m glad it turned out well.

avoid.right: Congrats to you!
avoid.why: Missing the preposition "to" makes the phrase ungrammatical.

functions.note: Match the register to how close you are to the person.

functions.name: Expressing preferences

formal: I would prefer to dine at a quieter restaurant.
My preference is to travel by train rather than by plane.
I would rather schedule the meeting for next week.
neutral: I like the chicken more than the fish.
I would rather stay at the hotel than a hostel.
I prefer coffee over tea.
informal: I’m more into pizza than burgers.
I’d rather chill at home tonight.
I’m keen on watching that new series.

responses: I agree, that option works better.

example.en: I would prefer to dine at a quieter restaurant.
I understand, there's a small bistro nearby.
Great, let's book a table there.
I'll make the reservation.

avoid.wrong: I prefer to eat fish more than chicken.
avoid.right: I prefer fish to chicken.
avoid.why: Use 'prefer X to Y', not 'more than' after 'prefer'.

functions.note: Use 'prefer' with 'to' or 'rather than' for clear comparisons.

functions.name: Expressing surprise and interest

formal: That is quite remarkable, please tell me more.
I must admit, that comes as a surprise.
How extraordinary! How did that happen?
neutral: Really? I had no idea about that.
That is amazing, tell me what happened next.
Are you serious? That sounds incredible.
informal: No way! You cannot be serious!
You are kidding! How did that go down?
Wow, that is wild! Tell me everything.

responses: I know, I could hardly believe it myself.
It is completely true, I promise.
That was my exact reaction when I heard.

example.en: I won first prize in the photography contest.
Are you serious? That sounds incredible.
I know, I could hardly believe it myself.
You definitely deserve it after all your hard work.

avoid.right: I am very surprised.
avoid.why: Use the past participle ending in -ed to describe your feeling.

functions.note: Use rising intonation and follow up with a question to show genuine engagement.

functions.name: Giving your opinion

formal: In my view, the project could benefit from more research.
From my perspective, the proposal seems viable.
I would suggest that we consider alternative options.
neutral: I think the meeting went well.
It seems to me that the deadline is realistic.
I believe this approach will work.
informal: I reckon it's a good idea.
Sounds like a plan to me.
I'm pretty sure it'll be fine.

example.en: I think the meeting went well.
That's an interesting point.
I also believe the agenda covered all key topics.
I see what you mean.

avoid.right: I think it is good.
avoid.why: A complete clause needs a subject after 'think'.

functions.note: Use 'I think' followed by a full clause to express personal opinions.

functions.name: Giving reasons and excuses

formal: I was unable to attend because I had a prior commitment.
Unfortunately, I missed the deadline due to unforeseen circumstances.
I regret that I cannot join, as I am unwell.
neutral: I couldn't come because I was busy.
Sorry, I missed it – my alarm didn’t go off.
I can’t make it, I have another meeting.

example.en: I couldn’t come because I was busy with another project.
I understand.
I’ll catch up on the notes later.
No worries, let me know if you need anything.

avoid.wrong: I didn't come cause I didn't want to.
avoid.right: I couldn't come because I had another appointment.
avoid.why: Blunt language sounds rude and unprofessional.

functions.note: Give a brief, plausible reason; avoid over‑explaining.

functions.name: Interrupting politely

formal: Excuse me, may I add something?
Pardon me, could I interject?
If I may, I'd like to comment.
neutral: Sorry to interrupt, but…
Can I just say something?
Excuse me, I have a point.

responses: Sure, what were you going to say?

example.en: Excuse me, may I add something?
Go ahead.
I think the deadline should be moved to Friday.
Noted, thank you.

avoid.right: Excuse me, may I interrupt?
avoid.why: Directly stating you want to interrupt sounds rude.

functions.note: Use "excuse me" to soften an interruption.

functions.name: Making a complaint

formal: I would like to make a complaint about the service.
Could you please address this issue?
I am dissatisfied with the service I received.
neutral: I’m not happy with this.
There seems to be a problem with my order.
Can I speak to a manager, please?

responses: Let me see how I can help.
I’ll do my best to resolve it.

example.en: I’m not happy with this, the meal was cold.
I’m sorry to hear that.
Could you bring a fresh dish, please?
Absolutely, I’ll arrange that right away.

avoid.wrong: I have a complaint about you.
avoid.right: I have a complaint about the service.
avoid.why: Complaints target the service, not the person.

functions.note: Stay calm and specific when lodging a complaint.

functions.name: Refusing a request politely

formal: I appreciate the offer, but I am unable to accept.
Regrettably, I have a prior commitment at that time.
I am afraid that will not be possible under the circumstances.
neutral: I would love to help, but I am really busy right now.
I am afraid I cannot make it this time.
Thanks for asking, but I already have plans.
informal: I would rather pass this time, if that is okay.
Sorry, I cannot swing it today.
I wish I could, but I am totally swamped.

responses: No problem at all, maybe next time.
That is completely understandable, do not worry.
Thanks for letting me know so quickly.

example.en: Can you help me move these boxes this weekend?
I would love to help, but I am really busy right now.
No problem at all, maybe next time.
Thanks for understanding, good luck with the move.

avoid.wrong: No, I do not want to.
avoid.right: I am afraid I cannot make it.
avoid.why: A flat 'no' sounds harsh; cushion the refusal with an apology or reason.

functions.note: Soften your refusal by expressing appreciation first, followed by a brief, general reason.

functions.name: Making special requests in a restaurant

formal: Could I please have the dressing on the side?
May I request a gluten‑free menu, please?
Would it be possible to have my steak cooked medium‑rare?
neutral: Can I get the sauce separate?
I’d like a vegetarian option, please.
Could you make my pasta less spicy?
informal: Can you leave the mayo off?
I want it not too hot.

example.en: Could I please have the dressing on the side?
Certainly, I’ll note that.
And could you make the soup a little less salty?
I’ll ask the chef and let you know.

avoid.right: Could I have the sauce on the side, please?
avoid.why: Polite phrasing is expected in restaurants.

functions.note: Use "could" and "please" for courteous requests.

functions.name: Disagreeing politely

formal: I see your point, however I must disagree on this matter.
While I respect your opinion, I have a different perspective.
I understand your argument, yet I believe the evidence suggests otherwise.
neutral: I’m not sure I agree with that.
That’s an interesting view, but I think otherwise.
I see what you mean, but I have a different take.

responses: I understand where you're coming from.

example.en: While I respect your opinion, I have a different perspective.
I see, could you explain your reasoning?
Certainly, the data shows a higher correlation with variable X.
That makes sense, thank you for clarifying.

avoid.right: I disagree with you.
avoid.why: 'Disagree' is a verb; it does not need the auxiliary 'am'.

functions.note: Stay respectful; focus on ideas, not the person.

functions.name: Making a request in a formal email

formal: I would be grateful if you could provide the requested documents by Friday.
Please could you forward the report at your earliest convenience?
Kindly send the required files no later than Friday.
neutral: Could you send me the documents by Friday?
Please forward the report when you have a chance.
I need the files by Friday; can you arrange that?
informal: Send me the docs by Friday, please.
Hey, can you shoot over the report?
Just get the files to me by Friday.

responses: Sure, I’ll have them to you by Thursday.
I’ll need a day extra; will that be okay?
I’m on it and will email them shortly.

example.en: I would be grateful if you could provide the requested documents by Friday.
Certainly, I will compile them and send them to you by Thursday.
Thank you; please let me know if any issues arise.
Will do, and I’ll confirm once they’re sent.

avoid.wrong: Give me the documents by Friday.
avoid.right: Please provide the documents by Friday.
avoid.why: Direct commands are too blunt for a formal email.

functions.note: Begin with ‘I would be grateful’ to show politeness.

functions.name: Giving constructive feedback

formal: I appreciate your effort, however, there are a few areas that could be refined.
Your work shows promise, yet some sections require further development.
The project is well-structured, though the conclusion could be stronger.
neutral: Good work, but you could improve the introduction.
Nice attempt; the analysis needs more detail.
Well done overall; the formatting could be tidier.
informal: Nice job, just tweak the intro a bit.
Looks good, but the ending feels rushed.
Cool effort, just polish the middle part.

responses: Thanks for the feedback; I’ll revise it.
I understand; I’ll focus on those sections.
Can you give me an example of the changes needed?

example.en: Good work, but you could improve the introduction.
Thanks, I’ll add more background information.
Make sure to link it clearly to the main argument.
Will do, I’ll rewrite that part.

avoid.right: Your work could be improved.
avoid.why: Negative wording discourages and is unconstructive.

functions.note: Combine praise with specific suggestions for balanced feedback.

functions.name: Inviting others to speak

formal: I would welcome any comments you may have.
Please feel free to share your thoughts.
We value your input on this matter.
neutral: Anyone have any ideas?
What do you think about this?
Feel free to add your view.

example.en: We value your input on this matter.
I think we could streamline the process.
That's a good suggestion.
We can discuss it further.

avoid.right: Please share your thoughts when you’re ready.
avoid.why: Too abrupt; invite politely.

functions.note: Open‑ended prompts encourage participation from all speakers.

functions.name: Negotiating a deadline

formal: Would it be possible to extend the deadline to…?
May I request an additional week to complete the work?
I propose we set the due date for…
neutral: Can we push the deadline to…?
I need a bit more time, maybe until…
Could we move the deadline back a few days?
informal: Can we get a few more days?
How about we finish it next week?
Let's stretch the deadline a bit.

responses: We'll need to check with the team.

example.en: Would it be possible to extend the deadline to next Friday?
That should be fine.
Thank you, I'll have the report ready by then.
Great, looking forward to it.

avoid.wrong: I can't do it, it's impossible.
avoid.right: I need more time to ensure quality.
avoid.why: Negative tone; offer a solution instead.

functions.note: Suggest a new date and give a brief reason.

functions.name: Softening an opinion with hedging

formal: It appears that the results may not meet our expectations.
One could argue that this approach is somewhat limited.
There is a possibility that we are overlooking an alternative.
neutral: I think the proposal could use some improvement.
It seems the data isn’t entirely reliable.
I feel the argument is a bit weak.
informal: Honestly, I’m not sure this works well.
To be fair, it’s kinda shaky.
I guess it’s not the best idea.

example.en: We’ve decided to stick with the current design.
There is a possibility that we are overlooking an alternative solution.
You may be right; let’s review other options.
Thanks, I’ll prepare some suggestions.

avoid.right: I think it might be problematic.
avoid.why: ‘Might’ provides a more natural hedge than ‘maybe’ after ‘I think’.

functions.note: Hedging softens statements and invites discussion.

functions.name: Taking and holding the turn

formal: If I may add something…
May I interject briefly?
Allow me to continue.
neutral: Can I say something?
Just a moment, please.
Hold on, I have a point.

example.en: May I interject briefly?
Go ahead.
I think the client needs more data in the report.
Please continue.

avoid.right: May I finish my thought?
avoid.why: Polite request avoids confrontation.

functions.note: Use turn‑taking markers to signal you want to speak.

functions.name: Announcing a change to a team

formal: I would like to inform you that, effective next Monday, we will be restructuring the project timeline.
Please be advised that the reporting procedure will be updated from the 15th of June.
Kindly note that the weekly meeting will now take place on Thursdays.
neutral: From next week, we’re moving the deadline up by two days.
We’re changing the way we submit timesheets starting tomorrow.
The team lunch will now be on Fridays instead of Wednesdays.
informal: Heads up – we’re shifting the launch date to next Thursday.
Just so you know, the coffee break is now at 10 am.
FYI, we’re swapping the parking spots today.

responses: Will the new schedule affect my tasks?

example.en: Please be advised that the reporting procedure will be updated from the 15th of June.
What changes should we expect?
All reports will now be submitted through the new portal.
Thanks, I’ll make sure to follow the new process.

avoid.right: We are going to change the schedule
avoid.why: Use the full form "are going to" for correct future construction.

functions.note: Begin announcements with "Please be advised" or "I would like to inform you" for a professional tone.

functions.name: Conceding a point gracefully

formal: You raise a compelling argument, and I must acknowledge its validity.
I concede that your suggestion has merit.
Upon reflection, I accept that your assessment is accurate.
neutral: You’ve got a point there.
I’ll admit that’s true.
Fair enough, I was wrong about that.
informal: Touché, I can’t argue with that.

responses: Glad we’re on the same page.

example.en: You’ve got a point there.
I’m glad you see it that way.
Let’s incorporate that into our plan.
Sounds good, moving forward then.

avoid.right: I was mistaken.
avoid.why: Avoid blunt self‑deprecation; acknowledge the specific point instead.

functions.note: Use 'concede' in formal settings; informal contexts favour simple admissions.

functions.name: Defusing a conflict

formal: Let’s step back and examine the issue calmly.
I propose we focus on a solution rather than assigning blame.
Perhaps we can find common ground on this matter.
neutral: Can we take a breath and talk this through?
Let’s try to keep things civil and sort it out.
How about we look at the facts together?
informal: Hey, let’s not blow this out of proportion.
Chill, we can sort this out.
Relax, it’s not worth fighting over.

responses: Okay, let’s work on a solution.

example.en: Can we take a breath and talk this through?
Absolutely, I think that will help.
Let’s focus on the facts and see where we agree.
Agreed, we can find a solution together.

avoid.right: I think we’re both misunderstanding each other.
avoid.why: Aggressive language escalates conflict; neutral phrasing de‑escalates.

functions.note: Using 'let’s' invites collaboration and reduces tension.

functions.name: Disagreeing diplomatically in a debate

formal: While I respect your perspective, I must point out that the evidence suggests otherwise.
I see merit in your argument, yet the data indicates a different conclusion.
With due respect, I find the premise somewhat flawed.
neutral: I understand your view, but I have a different take.
That’s an interesting point, however I see it another way.
I hear what you’re saying, yet I disagree on this aspect.
informal: I get where you’re coming from, but I’m not buying it.
Fair enough, but I think you’re off the mark.
No doubt, but I see it differently.

responses: I see your point, let’s consider both sides.
Alright, we can explore that further.

example.en: I understand your view, but I have a different take.
I appreciate your honesty; can you elaborate?
Certainly, the recent figures show a contrary trend.
That’s a compelling counter‑point.

avoid.right: I see things differently.
avoid.why: A diplomatic opening softens disagreement and keeps the tone courteous.

functions.note: Start with a concession before presenting your counter‑argument to stay polite.

functions.name: Pitching an idea

formal: May I propose a solution that could enhance our quarterly targets?
I would like to put forward a concept that addresses the current bottleneck.
Allow me to outline a proposal that may yield significant savings.
neutral: I have an idea that might help us improve the process.
What if we tried this approach?
I think this could work well for the team.
informal: Hey, I've got a thought that could sort this out.
How about we give this a go?
I've been thinking – why not try this?

responses: That sounds promising, let's explore it further.
I see the potential, but we need more data.

example.en: May I propose a solution that could enhance our quarterly targets?
That sounds promising, let's explore it further.
I can provide the cost‑benefit analysis by Friday.
I see the potential, but we need more data.

avoid.wrong: I think maybe we could possibly try this idea?
avoid.right: I think we could try this idea.
avoid.why: Avoid redundant hedging; it weakens the pitch.

functions.note: Use confident, concise language when presenting a new proposal.

functions.name: Answering a hostile question

formal: I understand your concern; let me clarify the facts.
With respect, the premise of your question is inaccurate.
Allow me to address the point you raised directly.
neutral: I see why you might think that, but here's what actually happened.
That's a fair question; here's the answer.
Let me explain why that isn't the case.
informal: Look, that's not how it works.
I get why you're upset, but here's the real story.

example.en: I understand your concern; let me clarify the facts.
I appreciate the clarification.
The data shows a 12% increase, not a decline.
That doesn't change my view.

avoid.right: I’m sorry, that information is not correct.
avoid.why: Avoid direct accusations; they heighten hostility.

functions.note: Stay calm, focus on facts, and keep the tone respectful.

functions.name: Changing the topic gracefully

formal: If I may, I'd like to steer the conversation towards...
Perhaps we could shift our focus to...
Allow me to redirect our attention to...
neutral: Speaking of that, have you heard about...
By the way, did you notice...
On a related note, let's discuss...
informal: Speaking of that, check this out...
Alright, enough about that, here's something cool...

example.en: By the way, did you notice the new policy changes?
Yes, I saw them. They seem quite significant.
Indeed, and they will affect how we handle client requests.
Thanks for bringing it up; we should plan accordingly.

avoid.wrong: I want to change the subject to...
avoid.right: I’d like to change the subject to...
avoid.why: 'I’d like' sounds more polite than the blunt 'I want'.

functions.note: 'By the way' signals a smooth transition without sounding abrupt.

functions.name: Mediating tension in a group

formal: May I suggest we explore a compromise that addresses both concerns?
Perhaps we could schedule a separate meeting to discuss this matter in depth.
I propose we temporarily set aside our differences to focus on the shared objective.
neutral: Let's try to find a middle ground here.
Can we agree on a solution that works for everyone?
How about we take a short break and then come back to this?
informal: Come on, let's not fight over this.
How about we just sort this out over a coffee?
Let's chill and figure it out together.

example.en: Let's try to find a middle ground here.
I agree, we should look for a solution that satisfies both sides.
How about we draft a plan that incorporates each of our main concerns?
That sounds reasonable; let's move forward with that.

avoid.wrong: We must to find a compromise.
avoid.right: We must find a compromise.
avoid.why: The infinitive 'to' is unnecessary after 'must'.

functions.note: Use 'compromise' as a noun or verb, not 'compromising' in this context.

functions.name: Making a sensitive public statement

formal: I wish to acknowledge the concerns raised and assure you that we are taking decisive action.
It is with deep regret that we address the recent events and commit to transparency.
We recognise the impact of this issue and are dedicated to remedial measures.
neutral: We understand the worries and are working on a solution.
I want to be clear about what's happening and what we plan to do.
Our team is taking steps to address the problem.
informal: Hey, we know things went wrong and we're fixing it.
Sorry about the mess— we're on it.
We messed up, but we're sorting it out.

example.en: I wish to acknowledge the concerns raised and assure you that we are taking decisive action.
We appreciate your transparency and look forward to seeing the improvements.
Our next steps will be communicated publicly within the week.
Thank you for keeping us informed during this time.

avoid.wrong: We are sorry for the problem and we will fix it soon.
avoid.right: We apologise for the problem and are taking steps to resolve it promptly.
avoid.why: 'Apologise' is more formal and appropriate than 'sorry' in public statements.

functions.note: Use 'apologise' and 'assure' for credibility in formal statements.

functions.name: Speaking on a special occasion

formal: Ladies and gentlemen, it is my distinct honour to address you on this momentous occasion.
I stand before you today humbled by the significance of this event.
Allow me to extend my heartfelt gratitude to all who have contributed.
neutral: I'm delighted to be here today to celebrate this special day.
Thank you all for gathering to mark this important moment.
It's a pleasure to share a few words on this wonderful occasion.
informal: Hey everyone, thanks for coming—this is awesome!
Wow, what a great day to be together!
Just wanted to say a big thanks for being here!

example.en: I'm delighted to be here today to celebrate this special day.
We’re thrilled to have you with us; the event wouldn’t be the same without you.
Your support means a lot, and I look forward to what we’ll achieve together.
Here’s to many more successes ahead!

avoid.wrong: I am happy to be here for this special day.
avoid.right: I’m delighted to be here today to celebrate this special day.
avoid.why: 'Delighted' conveys a more appropriate level of formality for speeches.

functions.note: Begin with a greeting, state purpose, and end with thanks.
